messages.subject: Quality assessment
parts:
Hi everyone,

thanks for your replies in the "FIRMA Scores" Thread.

Right now I had to go one step back and try to do the quality assessment a bit more carefully. Am I right, that the only 'built-in' methods to do so are the density plots, MvA-plots and spatial plots for the raw data and RLE und NUSE plots for the plm-summarized data, right? (Furthermore you could plot residuals, errrors, weights and so on for certain units.)

But I would also like to have boxplots for raw and normalized data. I made these plots by myself (because of memery-problems this was a bit tedious and the code went ugly...) but to my suprise the boxplots of the normalized data are not like expected. Shouldn't all boxes (one boxs corresponds to one chip) be aligned in a way that all medians are equal and the IQRs are all the same? I attached both boxplots ("boxplot_raw.png" and "boxplot_RBC,QN.png"). But it seems that the normalized and bg-corrected data doesn't differ that much from the raw data! (this is also suggested by the density plots, see attachments) What do I have to think about this? (Do you need the code for inspection?)

Furthermore I would like to inspect the residuals after the plm-fit in more detail. Let me clarify my understanding of residuals first. A residual e is the difference of a measured value y and an estimated value yhat. So in general you would calculate estimates (like in getCalculateResidualsFunction.ProbeLevelModel) with e = y - yhat. If you underestimate you'll get a positive residual, if you overestimate you'll get a negative residual. But since you store the residual values in the intensities-field of an ResidualFile (which inherits AffymetrixCelFile) the residuals have to be positive. And so the function getCalculateResidualsFunction.RmaPlm() calculates e = y / yhat. So an underestimated measure corresponds with a residual > 1 and an overestimated measure corresponds with a residual < 1. Am I right so far?

 Now if I would like to identify any spatial pattern for over- or underestimation I hoped I could just do
  rs <- calculateResidualSet(...)
  rf <- getFile(rs, idx=1)
  getImage(rf, transform=list(function(x){sign(x-1)}), palette=rainbow(256), tags="sign,rainbow")
to get some sort of two-color spatial plot.
(All probes that are not included in the cdf have an estimate of zero after the fit and so would be transformed here to -1, like all overestimates. But I would accept this for a first approach.)
But all this approach yields is a spatial plot with one color. Something must have gone wrong with this transformation. I also had a look at the getImage-code where the transformation takes place but couldn't solve my problem. Did anyone create those kinds of plots or does anyone have an idea? Also I would like to create spatial plots of only the positve residuals (here residuals > 1) and plots with only negative residuals... Since I'm not sure about how to manipulate the ResidualFile directly (and maybe this isn't a very good idea) the "transform" parameter appears to be the most promising way for me.

And finally I have a question regarding (plain and simple) spatial plots of the residuals generated with
    ...
    getImage(rf, palette=rainbow(256), tags="rainbow")
ALL my plots seem to be vertically divided (see attachment "I7R_028c02,residuals,rainbow.png"). I would guess, this is not a chip-quality problem (since this applies for all chips) but some sort of systematic error in the plm-fit or so. Any experience with that?

Thanks again in advance for any kind of support,
Frank Ziegner

parts:
Hi Frank.

Yes, we'll need the code for inspection ... and a 'sessionInfo()'
doesn't hurt.

My first impression is that you've normalized a subset of the probes
(e.g. by using the Ensembl CDF), but are plotting boxplots and
densities of the probes on the entire chip. That's a guess.

The PLM fits are done on the log2 scale, but stored in CEL files on
the 2^ scale since they have to be positive. So, if you do a
'readUnits' on a ResidualSet, you'll need to take a log2 to get any
interpretation. But, the calculation is definitely done as y - \hat
{y}, NOT y / \hat{y}.

I haven't done any spatial plots of residuals so I can't relate to
the details there. You'd want to take log2 regardless to put them on
a meaningful scale. I usually base most of my quality assessment on
RLE and NUSE plots.

About your vertically divided residual plots ... what CDF are you
using? Since the CEL files can only store one probe effect per
probe, if a probe is part of multiple probesets, then the residual
calculations can get screwed up. Not sure if this is related to your
problem, but its the first thing that comes to mind.

Cheers,
Mark

Hm, I'm not sure if I'm understanding you... By probe effect you mean

screwed up? For a given probeset $i$ you have one to four measured

residuals for a probe in a multiple probeset. And even if that would
be a problem, I can't see why this would result in such a vertically
divided plot...? I'm still at a loss here.

library(aroma.affymetrix)

# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
# setup dataset and chip names
# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
verbose <- Arguments$getVerbose(-8)
timestampOn(verbose)
setwd("C:/Dokumente und Einstellungen/ragast1/Desktop/Exon-Daten/
Kahle")
projectName <- "TDP"
chipType <- "HuEx-1_0-st-v2"

# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
# define CDF files (main + ensembl)
# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
cdfCore <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType(paste(chipType,
"core,A20071112,EP", sep=","))


# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
# define CEL set
# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName(projectName, chipType=chipType,
checkChipType=F, cdf=cdfCore)


# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
# background correction + quantile normalization
# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
bc <- RmaBackgroundCorrection(cs,tag=c("*","core"),addJitter=T)
csBC <- process(bc,verbose=verbose,force=FALSE)
qn <- QuantileNormalization(csBC, typesToUpdate="pm")
csN <- process(qn,force=FALSE,verbose=verbose)


# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
# fit probe level models
# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
plm_unmerged <- ExonRmaPlm(csN,
mergeGroups=FALSE,flavor=c("affyPLM"))
fit(plm_unmerged, verbose=verbose,force=FALSE)


# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
# calculate residuals
# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
rs_merged<-calculateResidualSet(plm_unmerged,verbose=verbose)


# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
# write spatial plots of residuals to file
# - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
lapply(rs_unmerged, writeImage, palette=rainbow(256), tags="rainbow")

> generic value because all CDF Files have the same dimensions

The CDF file is simply a collection of sets of probes, giving the physical
X,Y location of a particular probe on the chip. aroma.affymetrix simply
figures out which indices these correspond to (in the big 2560x2560 array)
and only operates on those. If you are interested to know more about them
(and you will if you ever need to make one), use the 'readCdf' function on
the CDF file and have a look at what info is stored there.

> background probes? Are these probes in any way used in aroma right

> (This is more for the future...)

spatial plots for exon array data, but thats not to say they are
uninformative. I'll try and see if I can recreate what you see.

>> About your vertically divided residual plots ... what CDF are you
>> using? Since the CEL files can only store one probe effect per
>> probe, if a probe is part of multiple probesets, then the residual
>> calculations can get screwed up. Not sure if this is related to your

>
> Hm, I'm not sure if I'm understanding you... By probe effect you mean
> probe affinity, right? This is stored once for all chips in the file
> "probeAffinities.CEL". But why can the residual calculation get
> screwed up? For a given probeset $i$ you have one to four measured
> signals/probes $y_ij$ with $1 \leq j \leq 4$. If you call
> ExonRmaPlm(...,mergeGroups=FALSE,...) you'll have only one estimate
> \hat{y_i} per probeset, right? (See code below for cdf-File
> specification) That is the idea of summarizing the data, or not? So
> how are the residuals PER PROBE calculated? $r_ij = y_ij - \hat{y_i}$
> I guess? And all residuals are stored in a seperate CEL file.
> So I would say, there is no problem in calculating (or storing) the
> residuals for a probe in a multiple probeset. And even if that would
> be a problem, I can't see why this would result in such a vertically
> divided plot...? I'm still at a loss here.

First of all, I don't think this is related to your problem, because you
are using the 'core' CDF created by Elizabeth and that has been checked to
not have probes in multiple probesets.

It's off topic now, but just so you understand what I mean about the probe
effects thing, I'll try to be more clear. Say y_{ij} is the data for
SAMPLE i (not probeset as you mention above) and probe j (j=1,...,4 for
example). Residuals are calculated as:

r_{ij} = y_{ij} - \hat{a}_i - \hat{p}_j

where a_i are the chip effects and p_j are the probe effects.
aroma.affymetrix comes along, fits these models separately for each probe
set and stores the a_i (in a _chipEffects.CEL file?) and p_j (in
probeAffinities.CEL). But, you can only store one probe effect for any
probe, so if a probe is part of multiple probesets, only one will get
stored. Since the residuals rely on these (in a later calculation where
everything is read back from the various CEL files), there can be
problems. I know of a way to avoid this whole problem as it pertains to
residuals (and that is to store the residuals as they are calculated from
the 'preprocessCore' routines instead of calculating them afterwards), but
that is not implemented yet.

Long winded answer.

Cheers,
Mark

Just a small comment that I've probably made before. But I'm really not sure what the value of providing an option that deals with this 'problem' (that we can't store multiple residuals per probe) -- though a warning might be nice. I can't think of situations where this is really interesting, though I'm sure someone can tell me. If the probe is legitimately mapping to more than one gene, say because of overlapping genes, then I don't think the overlap is going to be interpretable in terms of alternative splicing, unless you are sure that one gene is absolutely not expressed. I don't like the Affy option of rolling the genes together; I prefer throwing out such regions and keeping the genes distinct, particularly if you are just looking at core or ensembl probesets anyway.

Just a thought,
Elizabeth

First of all, I don't think this is related to your problem, because you
are using the 'core' CDF created by Elizabeth and that has been checked to
not have probes in multiple probesets.

It's off topic now, but just so you understand what I mean about the probe
effects thing, I'll try to be more clear.  Say y_{ij} is the data for
SAMPLE i (not probeset as you mention above) and probe j (j=1,...,4 for
example).  Residuals are calculated as:

r_{ij} = y_{ij} - \hat{a}_i - \hat{p}_j

where a_i are the chip effects and p_j are the probe effects.
aroma.affymetrix comes along, fits these models separately for each probe
set and stores the a_i (in a _chipEffects.CEL file?) and p_j (in
probeAffinities.CEL).  But, you can only store one probe effect for any
probe, so if a probe is part of multiple probesets, only one will get
stored.  Since the residuals rely on these (in a later calculation where
everything is read back from the various CEL files), there can be
problems.  I know of a way to avoid this whole problem as it pertains to
residuals (and that is to store the residuals as they are calculated from
the 'preprocessCore' routines instead of calculating them afterwards), but
that is not implemented yet.

Long winded answer.

Cheers,
Mark

Elizabeth,

Where we may want probes to be in multiple probesets is in a CDF that is transcript-based instead of gene-based.  For comparing specific transcripts instead of lumping them all into a gene for differential analysis.  I'm probably going to make one of these in the next round of Ensembl CDFs (I've just been reminded that Ensembl 49 is out).  Though, in this case, you are probably not interested in residuals, at least in the FIRMA sense, but it does create problems if you are interested in looking at the residuals for quality assessment purposes.

Mark
